summary: Examines the problems with packet size when tunnels such as IP-in-IP are used in the middle of a network. It covers whether large packets are fragmented and reassembled, whether Path MTU Discovery is used, and how to avoid the problem operationally, and compares solutions. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a router in the middle of the network wraps a packet in another packet, the result is too big for some links on the way. This memo explains the four ways to deal with that and why each one has a catch.

questions: how do tunnels handle large packets
when should you use path mtu discovery in tunnels
subtitle: What happens to a big packet when the middle of the network wraps it in another packet.

tldr.problem: When a router in the middle of the network tunnels a packet, the wrapped packet is bigger than the one it started as, so it may no longer fit through the path.
tldr.mechanism: The memo examines four ways out: fragment the wrapped packet and reassemble it at the tunnel end, tell the sources to send smaller packets, keep the backbone's links big enough that wrapping always fits, or split the original packet before wrapping it.
tldr.outcome: Each option has a catch: reassembly is hard at high speed, path MTU discovery is unreliable in IPv4, high MTUs need planning, and splitting the original packet works only in IPv4 and breaks the don't-fragment rule.

today: RFC 4459 is an Informational memo published in April 2006, and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating RFC. It is a study of the problem rather than a specification, and it points at other documents for the detailed designs of Path MTU Discovery and of the transition mechanisms themselves.

sections.title: The Problem With Tunnels And Large Packets
sections.content:
Many ways of putting one packet inside another have been specified over the years, for example IP-in-IP, Generic Routing Encapsulation, the Layer Two Tunneling Protocol, or IPsec in tunnel mode, any of which might run on top of IPv4, IPv6 or some other protocol and carry the same or a different protocol inside. All of them can be run so that the endpoints of the inner protocol sit next to the endpoints of the outer one, which is host-to-host tunnelling; with one set of endpoints co-located, which is host-to-router or router-to-host; or between the routers themselves for all or part of the traffic passing between them, which is router-to-router tunnelling.

All these share one issue. How does the source pick a maximum packet size so that the packets still fit, even after being wrapped, in the smallest maximum transmission unit on the path? And if the source cannot be influenced, what do you do to wrap them anyway? The memo sets out four answers. Fragment every wrapped packet that is too big and reassemble it at the tunnel endpoints. Signal the sources whose traffic will be wrapped to send smaller packets, using Path MTU Discovery. Make sure in that particular environment the wrapped packets will fit on all the paths, for example by using a backbone with an MTU above 1500. Or fragment the original packet so that the pieces, once wrapped, still fit, and reassemble them at the destination. That last option is only available for IPv4 under certain assumptions.

It is also common to run several layers of encapsulation, such as GRE or L2TP over IPsec, and with nested tunnels the endpoints may be the same or different and the inner and outer tunnels may use different strategies. The size problem is relatively straightforward in host-to-host and host-to-router tunnelling, where Path MTU Discovery only has to signal one source node. It is significantly harder in router-to-router and certain router-to-host cases, which are what the memo focuses on.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router in the middle of the network wraps a packet in another packet, the result is too big for some links on the way. This memo explains the four ways to deal with that and why each one has a catch.

sections.title: Fragment And Reassemble At The Tunnel Endpoints
sections.content:
The apparently simplest answer is to fragment the outer packet at the encapsulator and reassemble it at the decapsulator, but the memo says this is highly problematic for three reasons. Fragmentation causes overhead: every fragment needs the IP header, 20 or 40 bytes, and with IPv6 an additional 8 bytes for the Fragment header. Fragmentation and reassembly require computation, since splitting datagrams into fragments is not a trivial procedure and neither is reassembling them, and software router forwarding may not be able to do it at line rate. And at the time of reassembly, all the information is normally not available: when the first fragment arrives, a buffer of the maximum possible size may have to be allocated, because the total length of the reassembled datagram is not yet known, and since fragments may be lost, reordered or delayed, the reassembly engine has to wait with the partial packet for some time, for example 60 seconds. At line rate, with something like 10 Gbit/s, the buffers that reassembly would require would be prohibitive.

For router-to-router tunnelling the third problem is likely the worst. There is a further issue specific to IPv4: the identification header length is only 16 bits, compared to 32 bits in IPv6, so if a large number of packets are being tunnelled between two IP addresses the identification value is very likely to wrap and cause data to be misassociated. Reassembly wrongly combining data from two unrelated packets causes an integrity problem and potentially a confidentiality violation.

IPv6, and IPv4 with the don't-fragment bit set in the encapsulating header, let the tunnel endpoints optimize the tunnel MTU and minimize network-based reassembly, and also prevent fragmentation of the encapsulated packets on the tunnel path. If the IPv4 encapsulating header does not have that bit set, the tunnel endpoints will have to do a significant amount of fragmentation and reassembly, while the use of Path MTU Discovery is minimized. The worst case for how much has to be fragmented comes when the tunnel MTU is treated as infinite, or as equal to the physical interface MTUs.
sections.plainLanguage: Splitting the wrapped packet and putting it back together at the far end is the obvious answer, but every fragment costs another header, the work has to be fast enough for the link speed, and the far end may have to hold a large buffer for a long time while it waits for missing pieces.

sections.title: Signalling The Lower MTU To The Sources
sections.content:
The second approach is to use techniques such as Path MTU Discovery to tell the sources whose packets will be encapsulated to send smaller packets. When this is done on routers it has two separable functions. The forwarding behaviour: when forwarding packets, if the IPv4 don't-fragment bit is set, the router sends an ICMP Packet Too Big message to the source if the MTU of the outgoing link is too small. And the router's host behaviour: when the router receives an ICMP Packet Too Big message relating to a tunnel, it adjusts the tunnel MTU and originates an ICMP Packet Too Big message to the source address of the encapsulated packet, either immediately or when the next packet triggers one, the former minimizing packet loss.

This presupposes that Path MTU Discovery works. It currently works for IPv6 and is critical to its operation, but there is ample evidence that in IPv4 it is far from reliable, because firewalls and other boxes are configured to inappropriately drop all ICMP packets, or software bugs render it inoperational. Two scenarios make signalling from the network highly undesirable: when the encapsulation happens in such a prominent place that a very large number of sources would have to be signalled, possibly several times each; and when the encapsulation is done for passive monitoring purposes, where it is critical that the sources whose traffic is being wrapped do not know about it.

When the aim is to avoid fragmentation, IPv4 requires one of two alternatives: copy the don't-fragment bit from the inner packet to the encapsulating header, or always set the bit in the outer header. The latter is better, especially in controlled environments, because it forces Path MTU Discovery to converge immediately. A related technique that works with TCP under specific scenarios only is MSS clamping, where the tunnel endpoints reduce the TCP maximum segment size so that the connection automatically restricts itself to the maximum available packet size. That does nothing for UDP or other protocols that have no maximum segment size, and it assumes all the traffic passes through endpoints that do the clamping.
sections.plainLanguage: The network can tell the sender to use smaller packets, using an ICMP message. That works well in IPv6 but is unreliable in IPv4, where firewalls often block those messages, and it would be wrong to use it for traffic being watched in passing.

sections.title: Operational Planning And Splitting The Inner Packet
sections.content:
The third approach is operational. If a provider tunnels in a backbone made only of links with high MTUs, such as Gigabit Ethernet or SDH/SONET, while all its customers and peers have a lower MTU, then no wrapped packet would be larger than the backbone MTU and everything would fit. The memo calls this approach highly assumptive of the deployment scenario. It may be desirable to build a tunnel to another provider, where the assumption no longer holds; there may be links in the network that cannot support the higher MTUs; or the tunnel might be set up directly between the customer and the provider, in which case fragmentation would occur, with the wrapped fragments terminating on the provider and requiring reassembly from the provider's equipment. This approach can only be considered when tunnelling is done inside a part of a specific kind of provider's own network, not for example when transiting a provider.

A related idea is to have the sources use a low enough MTU to fit in all the physical MTUs, for example the IPv6 minimum MTU of 1280 bytes. That is not the case today and would be unrealistic to assume in general. It is worth remembering that even with IPv6 there are scenarios where the tunnel implementation must fragment and reassemble, such as an IPv6-in-IPv6 tunnel on top of a physical interface with an MTU of 1280 bytes, or two layers of IPv6 tunnelling. Because IP can be tunnelled on top of IP, no single minimum or maximum MTU can be found that would mean fragmentation or signalling to the sources is never needed.

The fourth possibility is fragmenting the inner packet before encapsulation so that the wrapped packet fits the tunnel's path MTU. Only IPv4 supports this in-flight fragmentation, and it is not allowed for packets where the don't-fragment bit has been set, and so many IPv4 host stacks send packets with that bit set that this would seem infeasible. There are existing implementations that violate the standard: discarding too big packets whose bit is not set instead of fragmenting them, which is rare; ignoring the bit completely, for all or specified interfaces; or clearing the bit before encapsulation on the egress of configured interfaces, which is typically done for all the traffic rather than only the too big packets. Clearing the bit effectively disables the sender's Path MTU Discovery for the path beyond the tunnel, which may result in fragmentation later in the network, though since the packets have already been fragmented before encapsulation that does not make matters significantly worse. This is non-compliant behaviour, but it has uses, especially in tightly controlled passive monitoring scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: Two more options: plan the network so wrapped packets always fit, or split the original packet before wrapping it. The first needs careful planning and only works inside one provider's own network. The second only works in IPv4 and breaks the rule that says a packet must not be split.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.content:
Fragmentation and reassembly by the tunnel endpoints is a clear and simple solution, but the hardware reassembly when packets get lost may face implementation challenges that prove insurmountable. It does not seem feasible for IPv4 at high data rates, because of the problem with the fragment identification field wrapping. Constant wrapping may occur when the data rate is in the order of MB/s for IPv4 and in the order of dozens of GB/s for IPv6. This approach is probably not a problem for passive monitoring applications.

Path MTU Discovery techniques, at least at the moment and especially for IPv4, appear too unreliable or unscalable to be used in backbones, and it is an open question whether a future solution might work better in that respect. It is clear that in some environments the operational approach, keeping higher MTUs in the networks where wrapped packets traverse, is sufficient, but that is unlikely to be enough in general, and for vendors who cannot assume anything about operators' deployments. Fragmentation of the inner packet is only possible with IPv4, and is sufficient only if standards-incompliant behaviour with potential for bad side effects is adopted; it should not be used if there are alternatives, and fragmenting the outer packet seems a better option for passive monitoring.

So if reassembly in the network must be avoided, there are basically two possibilities. For IPv6, use ICMP signalling or operational methods. For IPv4, packets whose don't-fragment bit is not set can be fragmented before encapsulation, with the encapsulating header setting that bit, and packets whose bit is set would need the bit cleared, which is non-compliant; this also minimizes the need for unreliable Internet-wide Path MTU Discovery. The memo ends by naming the two questions that matter: whether a higher MTU can be assumed in the high-speed networks that deploy tunnelling, and whether slower-speed networks could cope with software-based reassembly, less capable hardware-based reassembly, or the other workarounds.
sections.plainLanguage: The verdict is that there is no clean answer. IPv6 can lean on ICMP signalling. IPv4 has to choose between non-compliant tricks and a reassembly burden that gets worse the faster the link is.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document describes issues with packet sizes and in-the-network tunnelling, and says on its own it has no security considerations. It does add that the different solutions have characteristics that may make them more susceptible to attacks. A router-based fragment reassembly could easily lead to buffer memory exhaustion if an attacker sends enough fragments without sending all of them, so that the reassembly stalls until a timeout; such fragment attacks have already been used against firewalls and host stacks and need to be taken into account in implementations.

The cryptographic cost is also worth weighing, and it is typically more significant than software reassembly. If an outer fragment goes missing, no cryptographic operations have yet been performed; if an inner fragment goes missing, they have already been performed. Which approach is therefore preferable depends on whether cryptography or reassembly is already provided in hardware, and for high-speed routers one should be able to assume that if a router is doing relatively heavy cryptography, hardware support is already required.

The solutions using Path MTU Discovery, and therefore ICMP, also have to take ICMP attacks into account. An attacker could send ICMP Packet Too Big messages indicating a very low MTU, to reduce throughput or as a fragmentation and reassembly denial of service attack.
sections.plainLanguage: Each fix has its own attack. Holding half a packet in memory waiting for the rest is a way to fill a router up, and lying about the packet size in an ICMP message is a way to slow a connection down.

items.title: Fragment the outer packet
items.text: Split the wrapped packet to fit the path and reassemble it at the tunnel endpoint.

items.title: Signal the sources
items.text: Tell the sources whose traffic is being wrapped to send smaller packets, for example with Path MTU Discovery.

items.title: Keep the MTU high enough
items.text: Make sure the wrapped packets always fit, for example by using links with an MTU above 1500 in the backbone.

items.title: Fragment the inner packet
items.text: Split the original packet before wrapping it. Only IPv4 allows this, and only when the don't-fragment bit is not set.
